extra_misconceptions.fact: Colonial postmasters used handwritten rate marks in 1775; the United States issued its first official adhesive stamps in July 1847.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Benjamin Franklin issued the first adhesive United States postage stamps when the Second Continental Congress named him Postmaster General.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Universal Postal Union rules require Latin-letter country names except for Great Britain, which shows the reigning monarch's silhouette.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every sovereign nation prints its country name in English on its postage stamps to comply with Universal Postal Union rules.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Before 1847 stamps and mandatory prepayment in 1855, recipients usually paid the postage fee upon delivery based on sheet count and mileage.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Early American mail recipients always received letters for free because the sender paid the full postage at the origin post office.

extra_misconceptions.fact: The Pony Express was a private relay service that ran for only eighteen months between Missouri and California until October 1861.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The Pony Express operated as a nationwide government postal service for several decades across the nineteenth-century United States.

extra_socratic_questions: What postal change in 1847 shifted United States mail fees from recipient-paid mileage rates to prepaid adhesive stamps?
Which visual clue on a foreign stamp identifies its country of origin when the inscription uses a non-Latin alphabet?
Under what historical condition did Pony Express riders carry transcontinental mail before the telegraph replaced them?
Why did Great Britain omit its country name from the 1840 Penny Black and all subsequent British definitive postage stamps?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Topical collections group stamps by subject matter such as birds, Scouting, or trains across many countries and time periods.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A topical stamp collection must include every stamp ever issued by a single country in strict chronological catalog order.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Collectors prefer unaddressed First Day Covers with a clean First Day of Issue cancellation and a printed or engraved cachet artwork.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: First Day Covers only have philatelic value when the envelope carries a handwritten address from the original postmaster.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Postal stationery collectors save intact envelopes, aerogrammes, and postal cards that carry preprinted or embossed postage indicia.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Postal stationery collections consist strictly of loose adhesive stamps soaked off incoming commercial envelopes and postcards.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Because hundreds of thousands of stamps exist, worldwide collectors usually sample representative issues or limit their collection by era.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Worldwide collectors attempt to acquire every single stamp ever printed by every postal administration since May 1840.

extra_socratic_questions: What distinguishes a topical stamp collection focused on space exploration from a traditional worldwide country collection?
Which postmark feature confirms that an envelope qualifies as a genuine First Day Cover rather than ordinary used mail?
Where on a postmarked cover do postal clerks or sorting machines apply markings that a cancellation collector studies?
Why do specialized single-country collectors track subtle paper, watermark, and perforation varieties of the same stamp design?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Coil stamps dispensed from rolls naturally have two parallel straight edges and two opposite perforated edges for tearing.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Any stamp with two straight edges and two perforated edges was trimmed with scissors by a careless collector.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An overprint adds text or graphics for a new use, whereas a surcharge specifically alters or restates the stamp's face value.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Every overprint applied to the face of a stamp is also called a surcharge regardless of what the added ink says.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Only the base denomination on a semipostal stamp pays for postage; the extra fee goes to a fundraising cause set by law.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The charitable surcharge portion printed after the plus sign on a semipostal stamp pays for extra ounce postage weight.

extra_misconceptions.fact: All earliest nineteenth-century stamps were intentionally issued imperforate and had to be cut apart from the sheet with scissors.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Imperforate stamps are always modern printing errors where the perforating machine missed a sheet at the factory.

extra_socratic_questions: What physical difference separates a simple text overprint from a surcharge applied to an existing postage stamp?
Which edge pattern distinguishes a horizontal coil stamp from a single stamp torn out of a full post office pane?
What pricing structure on a semipostal stamp divides the buyer's payment between mail delivery and a designated charity?
Why do postal services print definitive stamps in multi-year runs while limiting commemorative stamps to short printings?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Catalog values estimate retail replacement cost for Fine-to-Very-Fine examples; dealers buy below catalog and discount flawed stamps.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The dollar value printed in a standard stamp catalog represents the exact cash price a dealer will pay to buy that stamp.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Condition depends on design centering, intact perforations, fresh color, absence of thins or creases, and gum state, not age alone.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A stamp's age is the primary factor that determines its condition grade and monetary value in the philatelic market.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Collectors prize light, neat cancellations that leave the stamp's engraved portrait and design details clearly visible.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Heavy black cancellation ink across the portrait makes a used stamp more valuable because it proves postal authenticity.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cutting off perforations creates a fraudulent straight edge that ruins the stamp's genuineness and destroys its collector value.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Trimming a pulled or ragged perforation tooth off the edge with scissors restores a damaged stamp to Very Fine condition.

extra_socratic_questions: What physical flaws on the front or back of a stamp reduce its grade from Very Fine to Fine or Average condition?
Which centering measurement compares the white paper margins around the printed design against the four perforated edges?
Under what market condition will a dealer sell a common stamp for a fraction of its listed Scott catalog valuation?
Why does a hinge remnant or a tiny paper thin on the back of a mint stamp sharply lower its retail market price?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A perforation gauge counts the number of perforation teeth or holes that fit within a standard two-centimeter span.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A perforation gauge measures the total number of perforation holes running along the entire length of a stamp's edge.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Serrated tweezers crush paper fibers and scratch gum, whereas stamp tongs have completely smooth, rounded or spade tips.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Household medical tweezers with serrated jaws work just as safely as philatelic stamp tongs for lifting rare stamps.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Most self-adhesive stamps use water-insoluble acrylic gum, so collectors trim closely around the paper backing instead of soaking.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Modern United States self-adhesive stamps release easily from envelope paper when soaked in a bowl of warm tap water.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Food bags trap moisture and leach softeners called plasticizers, while glassine is pH-neutral, breathable, and static-resistant.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Ordinary plastic sandwich bags protect sorted stamps just as safely as acid-free philatelic glassine envelopes.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement unit does a perforation gauge count when you align a stamp's teeth along its printed calibration tracks?
Why is it dangerous to handle mint stamps with bare fingers or ordinary steel tweezers instead of smooth philatelic tongs?
What happens to the dye in brightly colored envelope paper if you soak it in hot water alongside pale stamps?
Which hidden paper feature becomes visible when you place a stamp face down in a black tray with a drop of watermark fluid?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Excess moisture flows onto a mint stamp's original gum and bonds it to the page; only the tip of the hinge needs light dampening.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Licking an entire stamp hinge until it is dripping wet creates the strongest bond between the stamp and the album page.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Household tape and glue contain acids and migrating adhesives that turn brown, soak through stamp paper, and ruin the stamp.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Clear household cellophane tape or white school glue provides a safe, archival way to mount stamps onto album pages.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Ultraviolet light from direct sunlight bleaches sensitive stamp inks and makes album paper brittle and yellow within weeks.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Displaying a stamp album open near a sunny window keeps the paper dry and brightens faded printing inks.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Heavy flat stacks press stamps against opposite pages and cause sticking in humidity; binders should stand upright with support.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stacking heavy stamp albums flat in a tall pile protects the pages better than standing binders upright on a bookshelf.

extra_socratic_questions: Why should a collector mount Mint Never Hinged stamps in clear archival sleeves rather than moistening a gummed stamp hinge?
Where on the back of a used stamp should you position the short folded flap of a slightly moistened philatelic hinge?
What happens to original water-activated stamp gum when albums are stored in a humid basement or damp attic?
Which chemical hazard in cheap cardboard, school glue, or cellophane tape permanently stains stamp paper over time?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A cachet stays on the left side of the envelope, leaving the upper right for the stamp and the lower right for the postmark or address.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A decorative cachet design should cover the entire front of an envelope so the artwork stands out in an album.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Fine lines and tiny lettering blur together at one-inch stamp scale, so designers use bold contrast, simple shapes, and clear type.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A stamp design drawn on a large poster sheet will automatically remain readable when reduced to actual postage stamp size.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A bourse is an open marketplace of dealer tables where collectors of all levels browse stockbooks, covers, and bargain boxes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The dealer bourse at a stamp show is a private auction room reserved strictly for museum curators and wholesale buyers.

extra_misconceptions.fact: United States postal policy prohibits honoring living individuals on stamps, requiring subjects to be deceased for at least three years.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: The Citizen's Stamp Advisory Committee accepts requests to print living politicians and celebrities on United States stamps.

extra_socratic_questions: What essential elements must appear on a functional postage stamp design besides the central illustration?
Where on a First Day Cover envelope does a cachet artist leave open space so the artwork will not block postal markings?
What separates the competitive exhibit frames from the dealer bourse tables when you walk through a regional stamp show?
Which graphic details in a pictorial handstamp cancellation tie the postmark to the host city or anniversary event?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Requirement 8 specifies different stamps, meaning each stamp must be a distinct issue or recognizable catalog variety, not a duplicate.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Mounting fifty identical Forever flag stamps on a page counts as fifty stamps toward the merit badge collection requirement.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Thin notebook paper tears at the rings and contains wood-pulp acid; homemade pages need heavyweight, acid-free cardstock.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Ordinary three-ring notebook filler paper makes a durable, archival page for mounting a permanent stamp collection.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leaving generous margins, straight rows, and brief captions gives each stamp visual breathing room and makes pages easy to inspect.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Crowding thirty or forty stamps edge-to-edge onto every album page creates the cleanest presentation for a counselor review.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Ballpoint ink indents paper fibers and bleeds through to the front; notes belong on the album page or in light pencil on a mount.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Inscribing catalog numbers and country notes directly on the backs of stamps in ballpoint pen keeps a collection organized.

extra_socratic_questions: What layout technique keeps a homemade album page balanced before you fasten a single hinge or mount to the paper?
Why do two stamps of the exact same design count as only one stamp toward the 250-stamp minimum unless a variety differs?
Where should you place country captions or leader lines on a 50-country map display when tiny nations cluster together?
Which paper weight and archival standard prevent homemade album pages from sagging in a binder or toning your stamps?
